A single label. Millions of patients. Zero room for error.
Context

Everything starts
with one label.

Take this bottle. Paracetamol Paediatric Oral Suspension. A common medicine for children. Before it reaches a pharmacy shelf, its label must pass through a complex regulated lifecycle — and every step is a potential failure point.

💊
Active ingredient & dosage
Paracetamol 240mg/5ml — must match approved formulation exactly. Any error risks patient harm.
🌐
Multi-language & regional compliance
Labels must carry warnings in local scripts and meet regional regulatory bodies — EU 2019/6, WHO, CDSCO, and others simultaneously.
📊
Barcode & serialisation
GS1 barcode, batch number, expiry — machine-readable and human-readable. A single pixel offset can fail a scan.
⚠️
Regulatory warnings
Mandatory symbols, contraindications, storage conditions — governed by law in every market.
International label compliance — languages this label must support
EN English
हि Hindi
తె Telugu
ಕ Kannada
த Tamil
മ Malayalam
বা Bengali
ਪੰ Punjabi
مر Marathi (Devanagari)
عر Arabic (MENA markets)
FR French (EU / Africa)
DE German (EU)

Each language variant requires its own artwork review and regulatory sign-off — multiplying the complexity of every single label change across markets.

Problem Statement

The process was
as risky as the label itself.

When I joined the project, Kallik had three product efforts running in parallel — an artwork editor, a file management system, and an early AI validation concept. None of them connected. Teams were stitching them together with email, shared drives, and manual sign-offs.

Before: Different tools. Different worlds. Same label. No single source of truth.

📁
Version chaos
Designers maintained personal naming conventions — Final_v2_ACTUALLY_FINAL.ai — because the system had no version control. Nobody knew which file was the source of truth.
"I have a folder called Final. Inside it is another folder called Actually Final." — Artwork Designer
📧
Invisible approval pipeline
Reviews and approvals happened entirely in email threads. Rowan — who carried both reviewer and approver responsibilities — had no structured workflow, no queue visibility, and no audit trail.
"I reply 'Approved' via email. There's no record of which version I checked." — Regulatory Reviewer
🤖
Untrusted AI
An early AI validation pass existed but was consistently ignored. It flagged issues without citing the regulation, providing a confidence level, or explaining the fix. Reviewers closed it rather than act on it.
"If AI says 'Possible Error' with no reason — I ignore it. I can't act on something I don't understand." — Rowan
🖨️
Print uncertainty
Print operators received files via email with no confirmation that the version was approved, validated, or even current. Every print run began with the question: "Is this definitely the right file?"
"Nobody could give me a straight answer." — Finn, Print Operator
4–6h
Manual review time per label per market
3
Disconnected products with no shared data model
0%
AI validation action rate — every flag was ignored
∞
Version variants circulating in email and shared drives
User Research

Understanding
80+ people across
three workflows.

Research spanned two phases across the product lifecycle. The goal was not just to understand pain points, but to map the artwork's journey as a shared object — and understand how each role's mental model broke down at every handoff.

Research methods
🎤
Contextual Interviews
One-on-one sessions with each role group. Participants walked through their most recent label workflow in full detail — actions, decisions, emotions, and workarounds. Designed to surface hidden complexity, not just stated preferences.
48 sessions · 3 role groups
🗺️
Workflow & Journey Mapping
End-to-end artwork journey mapped across all handoff points — from creation through multi-language review, regulatory sign-off, and final print release. Identified exactly where the artwork "lost its identity" between tools.
6 workflow maps · 3 product areas
🃏
Card Sorting
Used with regulatory reviewers to understand how they mentally organised compliance rules, confidence levels, and AI outputs. Directly informed the three-level validation indicator design (High / Review / Flag).
8 participants · validation IA
🧪
Moderated Usability Testing
Two rounds of testing — wireframes to validate flow logic, then high-fidelity prototypes to test AI transparency, status visibility, and approval workflows. All three role groups tested in both rounds.
2 rounds · all roles · 400+ data points
What each role told us — click to explore
🎨 Artwork Designer
"I've got a folder called CORRECT FINAL VERSION. Inside it there's another folder called ACTUALLY FINAL. That's our version control."
No version history in the system — personal file naming was the only version control across 40+ active label variants
File locking done informally via Slack messages — "I'm in the file" — with no system enforcement, leading to parallel edits
No visibility into review status once artwork entered the email chain — designs disappeared and feedback arrived without context
Required Pro editor tools: keyboard shortcuts, layer management, position controls, and full typography precision
🔬 Reviewer & Approver — dual responsibility
"If the AI tells me why it flagged something and shows me the rule, I'll act on it every time. If it just says 'check this' — I'll close it."
Manual checklist review took 4–6 hours per label variant — multiplied across every language and regional market
Maintained 14 personal regulatory reference documents across markets (EU, India CDSCO, WHO) because no system held this context
AI validation was actively ignored — not because of distrust in AI, but distrust in AI that couldn't show its reasoning
After reviewing, approval was an email reply — no structured workflow, no record of which version was signed off, no audit trail
No queue visibility — had no way to see what was waiting, what was urgent, or what was blocked pending his input
🖨️ Print Operator — receives and prints only
"Is this definitely the right file? Nobody could ever give me a straight answer."
Received files via email with no confirmation the version was approved, AI-validated, or compliance-checked
No print specification attached — had to chase Aria or Rowan to confirm dimensions, quantity, and printer settings
Occasionally printed the wrong version because email approval threads were ambiguous about which file was final
Had no visibility into the compliance or validation status of the artwork he was about to send to press
Research Synthesis & Hypothesis

The pattern
beneath the
complaints.

Initially every role described a different problem. Designers wanted version control. Reviewers wanted trustworthy AI. Print operators wanted certainty. But the synthesis revealed a single underlying cause.

"The artwork never changed. Only the perspective changed.

Creation needed flexibility.
Review and approval needed confidence and structure.
Print needed certainty.

Treating these as three separate tools made every handoff a breaking point.
The design needed one shared artwork backbone — with role-specific surfaces."
Root cause
Fragmentation — the same artwork moving through different tools, losing its identity and traceability at every transition. Every handoff was a trust failure.
Multi-language impact
Each language variant required the full review cycle. With 12+ scripts and regional regulatory bodies, fragmentation wasn't a minor inefficiency — it was an exponential risk multiplier.
Design hypothesis
If we create one shared artwork backbone — where Aria creates, Rowan reviews and approves with AI support in-context, and Finn receives only validated released files — we can eliminate version conflicts, make compliance trustworthy, and reduce multi-market label cycle time by over 80%.
Design Process

How we moved from
research to platform.

The project followed an adapted Double Diamond process, with a deliberate emphasis on systems thinking before screen design. The shared data model, status architecture, and permission structure were defined before any interface work began.

1
Discover
Contextual research across all three workflows
48 interviews, 6 workflow maps, on-site shadowing across artwork studios, regulatory review rooms, and factory print floors. Goal: understand the artwork's full journey, not individual tool frustrations.
↳ Research report · Journey maps · 400+ synthesised findings
2
Define
Shared data model & status architecture first
Before any screen design, defined the shared artwork object, permission model, and six status states (Draft → In Review → AI Validated → Approved → Released → Archived). This prevented weeks of rework later and gave engineering a stable foundation.
↳ Data model · Permission matrix · Status taxonomy · IA map
3
Ideate
AI capability mapping & feature prioritisation
Ran an AI capabilities × validated user needs workshop. Mapped every potential AI feature against research findings. This kept the feature set purposeful — AI only where it solved a validated problem, not where it added complexity for its own sake.
↳ AI opportunity map · Feature priority matrix · Design principles
4
Design
Role-specific surfaces on one shared backbone
Designed the Pro Editor (Aria), the AI Validation + Review + Approval surface (Rowan), the Release module (Finn), and the shared Artwork Library. Built a unified design system covering comments, approvals, alerts, and AI patterns — designed once, applied across all six product areas.
↳ High-fidelity prototypes · Design system · 6 product surfaces
5
Test & Iterate
Two rounds of moderated usability testing
Round 1 on wireframes validated flow logic and IA. Round 2 on high-fidelity prototypes validated AI transparency, approval UX, and status visibility. Four key iterations emerged: Simple mode pruned by 40%, status pill replaced by colour-coded left border, confidence percentage replaced by H/R/F indicator (tripled action rate), override field added for audit compliance.
↳ Usability test reports · 4 key iteration decisions · Validated prototype
6
Deliver
Platform launch + design system handoff
Delivered a unified platform covering Create → Manage → Review → Validate → Approve → Release, with a full design system covering all six product areas. Post-launch: zero version conflicts, 91% AI validation action rate, 4 new enterprise customers in 3 months.
↳ Production-ready specs · Design system · Component library · Handoff docs

AI features designed inside the Kallik platform
🏷️
NLP Label Validation
Reads label copy against regional regulatory databases. Flags missing mandatory text, incorrect dosage phrasing, and non-compliant warning structures. Cites the specific regulation and clause for each issue.
In-product · Validation engine
👁️
Computer Vision Inspection
Scans artwork for barcode integrity, symbol placement, minimum font sizes across scripts, and colour contrast ratios. Runs against the master artwork template and flags deviations on the canvas directly.
In-product · Visual inspection
🌐
Multi-language Compliance Check
Validates that all required languages are present for a given market, checks script rendering quality, and flags missing regional regulatory symbols (e.g., red triangle for Schedule H drugs in India).
In-product · Regional compliance
Note: AI tools in my design workflow were used to accelerate research synthesis, documentation, and communication — not to replace judgement, user research, or design decisions. All strategic design choices were made through direct user engagement and validated through testing.
Solution Design

One connected platform.
Six lifecycle stages.

Instead of three disconnected products, we designed one governed platform with a single shared artwork object at its core. Every role-specific surface connects to the same artwork, status model, and audit trail.

Kallik Veraciti™ — bi-directional PLM/ERP integrations, intelligent rules engine, AI-driven AToM, review & approval, and print distribution

Key design decisions — expand each
01
Pro editor with auto-versioning — no more Final_Final files
+
Aria gets a full-capability Pro editor with canvas control, layer management, typography precision, and keyboard shortcuts. Every save creates an immutable version — timestamped, attributed, and linked to the artwork record. The informal Slack-message file locking was replaced with a smart lock system showing owner, duration, and estimated release time. Finn never touches the editor — he only receives released files through the Release module.
↳ 0 version conflicts post-launch
02
Inline AI validation — rule-cited, confidence-scored, on the canvas
+
The AI validation layer was designed to appear directly on the artwork canvas — not as a separate report. Each flag shows: the specific regulation being violated (e.g., EU 2019/6 Annex I, Section 3.2), a plain-English explanation of why it matters, a three-level confidence indicator (High / Review / Flag — replacing an ignored percentage number), and an inline suggested fix with an override field for audit documentation.

The confidence percentage was replaced after Round 1 testing showed it was being universally ignored. The three-level indicator tripled the action rate on flagged items.
↳ 91% compliance errors caught pre-print · 3× AI action rate
03
Rowan's unified review + approval workflow with full audit trail
+
Rowan's two responsibilities — regulatory review and production approval — were unified into one structured in-platform workflow. He reviews against AI-surfaced issues directly on the canvas, adds inline comments on the latest version (never on a PDF printout), and approves with one click. The system automatically records: which version was approved, which AI checks passed, any override reasons documented, and a timestamp. Aria is notified instantly. The approval is immutable and audit-ready.
↳ Review + approval in one place · Audit trail by default
04
Status-led navigation — Draft, Review, Approved, Released as primary IA
+
Status states became the primary navigational model — not module navigation or flat file lists. Both Aria and Rowan navigate by status: what needs action, what's waiting, what's approved. The artwork library replaced a generic file list with status-filtered views and a colour-coded left border on each row (replacing a status pill that Round 1 testing showed went entirely unread).
↳ Status visible at a glance · No inbox archaeology
05
Release module — Finn receives only what Rowan confirmed
+
Only artwork that has completed the full lifecycle — AI validated, compliance-checked, approved by Rowan — can reach the Release stage. Finn's view shows only released artwork, with print specifications pre-attached (quantity, dimensions, colour profile, printer settings) and a visible audit chain confirming who approved it, which version, and when. The question "Is this the right file?" is structurally impossible to ask.
↳ Finn prints with 100% version certainty
Key screens

Draft, In Review, Approved, Released as navigational anchors. Rowan sees his full queue without opening a single email.

Learnings & Next Steps

What this project
taught me.

Four principles distilled from 18 months of enterprise SaaS design, research, and iteration across regulated artwork operations.

01
Design the shared data model before the first screen. Defining the artwork object, permission structure, and six status states early gave engineering a stable foundation and prevented weeks of structural rework. In enterprise SaaS, architecture is UX.
02
AI trust is earned through transparency, not capability. Rowan ignored the original AI — not because it was wrong, but because it couldn't show its work. Once every flag included a regulation citation, confidence level, and suggested fix, his action rate went from 0% to near-total. The design challenge wasn't adoption. It was legibility.
03
Multi-language complexity must be designed in, not patched on. Each language variant multiplied every process inefficiency. The platform's governance model — one shared artwork, role-specific surfaces, AI validation per script — made international label operations tractable rather than exponentially complex.
04
The last person in the chain defines whether the system worked. If Finn still had to ask "Is this the right file?" after the platform launched, every upstream decision would have failed. Designing Finn's endpoint with certainty as the non-negotiable outcome — and working backwards from it — shaped every upstream architecture decision.

Next steps

Analytics layer for artwork operations — cycle time by market, bottleneck detection, and regulatory compliance trend reporting across all label variants
Automated multi-language rule set management — AI maintains regional regulatory databases, reducing Rowan's 14-document personal reference library to zero
Mobile review and approval companion for Rowan — queue visibility and one-tap approval on the factory floor without requiring desktop access
Closing

The most important
feature in regulated
industries is trust.

"By transforming three disconnected products into one governed platform, we didn't just improve usability. We created a system that Aria, Rowan, and Finn could each trust — for different reasons, in different ways, at different stages. In industries where a label error can reach a patient, that trust is not a design preference. It is the product."
